```{r walkdata}
#filtered_walk <- walkathon[which((walkathon$name %in% extra_walk$name)),]
filtered_walk <- walktober

# Read in extra walk and add in suburbs
extra_walk <- read.csv("data/extrawalktober.csv") |>
  mutate(suburb = ifelse(suburb == "Claython north", "Clayton", suburb),
         suburb = ifelse(suburb == "Clayton ", "Clayton", suburb),
         suburb = ifelse(suburb == "Mordi ", "Oakleigh", suburb),
         suburb = ifelse(suburb == "Oakleigh ", "Oakleigh", suburb),
         suburb = ifelse(suburb == "Langwarrin", "Mordialloc", suburb),
         suburb = ifelse(suburb == "Croydon", "Mordialloc", suburb))
#required_subs <- unique(c(extra_walk$suburb))
suburbs <- readRDS("data/suburbs.rds")

my_suburbs <- suburbs |> 
  filter(state_name_2021 == "Victoria") |>
  mutate(suburb_name_2021 = str_remove(suburb_name_2021, " \\(Vic.\\)")) |>
  filter(between(cent_long, 144.8, 145.2),
         between(cent_lat, -38, -37.8)) |>
  #filter(suburb_name_2021 %in% required_subs) |>
  #select(c(suburb_name_2021, geometry)) |>
  rename("suburb" = "suburb_name_2021")

extra_walk <- extra_walk |>
  left_join(my_suburbs, by = "suburb")
# add team colours
extra_walk$team_colour <- c(sequential_hcl(4, palette = "Peach"),
  sequential_hcl(5, palette = "Blues")[1:4],
  sequential_hcl(6, palette = "Reds 3")[2:5],
  sequential_hcl(5, palette = "Greens")[1:4],
  sequential_hcl(4, palette = "Purp"),
  sequential_hcl(8, palette = "Heat")[3:6])

# clean data to just local suburbs
clean_walk <- filtered_walk |>
  left_join(extra_walk, by="name") |>
  mutate(steps_dist = dist_normal(steps, 0.1*steps),
         date = as.Date(date, "%d/%m/%y")) |>
  group_by(name) |>
  mutate(cum_steps = cumsum(steps)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(date <= as.Date("23/10/25", "%d/%m/%y")) |>
  na.omit()
# remove emojis
clean_walk$team <- gsub("\\p{So}", "", clean_walk$team, perl = TRUE)
suburb_walk <- clean_walk |>
  as.tibble() |>
  group_by(suburb) |>
  summarise(mean_steps = mean(steps),
            steps_dist = dist_truncated(dist_normal(mean(steps), 0.1*mean(steps)), 0)) |> 
  left_join(my_suburbs, by = "suburb") |>
  select(c(suburb, steps_dist, mean_steps, geometry))


```

## Into the melting pot
Our current "decision making" framework sees these approaches as synonymous. Are they? 

![](images/meltingpot.jpg){fig-align="center"}


## Signal vs noise
::: {.incremental}
- The decision making framework obfuscates two disparate roles uncertainty can take on in our analysis
- **Uncertainty as signal**: we are interested in uncertainty as a statistic in it's own right
  - e.g. extracting variance or probabilities
- **Uncertainty as noise**: we are interested in how uncertainty affects our primary estimate
  - e.g. ensuring the signals are valid, preventing false conclusions
  
::: 

## Most research evaluates uncertainty as signal

![](images/signalnoisestudy.jpg){fig-align="center"}



## This creates conflict in the literature {.smaller}
::::: columns
::: {.column width="35%"}

![](images/idk.jpg){fig-align="center"}

:::

::: {.column width="65%"}

:::: {.incremental}
- This is a problem for cases where we want to visualise uncertainty as noise
- Evaluating uncertainty as signal (when it is supposed to be noise) can lead to the opposite conclusions [@Mason2026]
- Such as...
  - suggesting that we **ignore uncertainty** in high variance scenarios to **improve trust** [@Zhao2023], or
  - **questioning if we should even visualise uncertainty as all** [@MacEachren2005]

:::: 

:::
:::::

# How to evaluate uncertainty as noise?


## Why is it all signal?{.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

:::: {.incremental}

- Existing research uses explicit testing methods
- There are two ways to evaluate a plot [@Vanderplas2020]
  - Explicit: Viewer is directed to the purpose of the plot with a question
    - e.g. "What is the spatial correlation in this plot?"
  - Implicit: User must identify the purpose of the plot
    - "Identify the odd one out" (e.g. a lineup protocol [@Buja2009])
  
:::: 



:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center


# Generate true data from lineup protocol
data(wasps)

wasp.lda <- lda(Group~., data=wasps[,-1])
wasp.ld <- predict(wasp.lda, dimen=2)$x
true <- data.frame(wasp.ld, Group=wasps$Group)

# Generate lineup protocol plot
wasp.sim <- data.frame(LD1=NULL, LD2=NULL, Group=NULL, .n=NULL)
for (i in 1:19) {
  x <- wasps
  x$Group <- sample(x$Group)
  x.lda <- lda(Group~., data=x[,-1])
  x.ld <- predict(x.lda, dimen=2)$x
  sim <- data.frame(x.ld, Group=x$Group, .n=i)
  wasp.sim <- rbind(wasp.sim, sim)
}

pos <- sample(1:20, 1)
d <- lineup(true=true, samples=wasp.sim, pos=pos)

ggplot(d, aes(x=LD1, y=LD2, colour=Group)) + 
  facet_wrap(~.sample, ncol=5) +
  geom_point() + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(aspect.ratio=1,
        legend.position = "bottom") +
  scale_color_gdocs()
```

:::
:::::

## Which approach?
:::: {.incremental}
- Explicit approaches are the most common
- They also create two problems for uncertainty visualisation
  1. They evaluate uncertainty as signal
  2. They violate my Ratatouille rule
  
:::: 

## Which approach?

- Explicit approaches are the most common
- They also create two problems for uncertainty visualisation
  1. **They evaluate uncertainty as signal**
  2. They violate my Ratatouille rule

## Exploring versus Inference 
::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

:::: {.incremental}

- The way you with a plot can change what they see
  - e.g. people are worse at seeing dinosaurs if you give them an explicit task [@Boger2021]
- A similar problem occurs in uncertainty visualisation
  
:::: 



:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(datasaurus_dozen_wide, aes(x = dino_x, y = dino_y))+
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "X", y = "Y") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(aspect.ratio=1)
```

:::
:::::




## Evaluating uncertainty as signal
:::: {.incremental}

- The signal is not an inherent feature of the plot
- Signal is whatever we are drawing inference on
  - It is determined by the question you ask 
- Asking direct questions about variance or probability will turn the uncertainty into signal
  - This will occur regardless of the reason the plot was made

  
:::: 


## Can we use an implicit method?{.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}

:::: {.incremental}

- Can we use the lineup protocol?
  - Usually, yes. For uncertainty visualisation? No
- Think of it like this:
  - A lineup protocol is a visual hypothesis test
  - an uncertainty visualisation is a visual confidence interval
- They are different forms of inference and cannot be used to validate each other
- Confidence intervals require a question to be meaningful
  - Therefore we must have a question
  - This explains why all existing studies use explicit methods 
  
:::: 

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

![](images/hypvsconf.jpeg){fig-align="center"}

:::
:::::



## So what does evaluating uncertainty as noise look like? {.smaller}
::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}

:::: {.incremental}
- Instead we will evaluate plots on how well they perform **signal modulation**
  - The higher the variance on an estimate, the harder that estimate is to extract from the plot
- We measure uncertainty as an effect on a different signal variable that we ask about directly
  - This allows us to measure uncertainty as a *latent variable* 

:::: 

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

![](images/noisesignal2.jpeg){fig-align="center"}

:::
:::::


## Which approach?

- Explicit approaches are the most common
- They also create two problems for uncertainty visualisation
  1. They evaluate uncertainty as signal
  2. **They violate my Ratatouille rule**

## The Ratatouille rule{.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="65%"}

:::: {.incremental}

- We also want to avoid conflating  *understanding* with *seeing*
- "Not everyone can become a great artist, but a great artist can come from anywhere." - Anton Ego (Ratatouille (2007))
- "Not *everyone* need to be able to understand your plot, but a good plot can be understood by *anyone*. - Me (right here, right now)
  - Should not be limited by inherent ability (e.g. colour blindness)
  - Can be limited by actual skill/knowledge (e.g. what does spatial autocorrelation look like?) 

:::: 


:::

::: {.column width="35%"}

![](images/rats.jpeg){fig-align="center"}

:::
:::::



## Therefore we want an evaluation method that can...
:::: {.incremental}

1. Work for choropleth maps 
2. Measures uncertainty as a latent variable 
3. Is simple enough that it could be understood by a child 

:::: 


## ... Wait 
  
::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
:::: {.incremental}
- Isn't that just an Ishihara colour blind test?
  - Choropleth map
  - Measures latent variable (colour vision deficiency)
  - Is understood by children

::::

:::

::: {.column width="40%"}

![](images/ishi.png){fig-align="center"}

:::
:::::

## The data

```{r}

set.seed(731)
# generate data
D = c(0,1,2,3,4)
V = c(1,2,3,4,5)
Dlab = D
Vlab = V

# make data for plotting
parent_dists <- expand_grid(D, V) |>
  mutate(Background = dist_normal(-0.5*D, 1),
         Number = dist_normal(0.5*D, 1)) |>
    pivot_longer(cols = Background:Number,
               names_to = "group",
               values_to = "dist") 

estimate_dists <- gen_data(D, V, parentV = 1, noiseV = 0, number = 2) |>
  mutate(group = ifelse(group=="out", "Background", "Number")) |>
  group_by(D, V, group) |>
  slice_sample(n = 20) |>
  ungroup() |>
  rename("dist" = "estimate_dist") 

# set colours
pal <- colour("high contrast")(3)[c(2,1)]

# plot distributions
parent_dists |>
  ggplot(aes(xdist = dist, colour = group)) +
  
  # Visualise parent distribution
  stat_slab(scale = 0.3, fill=NA, 
            linewidth=1, alpha=0.5,
            aes(y=-0.35)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -0.35, colour = "black") +
  
  # Visualise Estimate Distribution
  stat_slab(data = estimate_dists, normalize = "panels",
             fill=NA, linewidth=0.2, alpha=0.3) + 
  labs(y = "Standard Deviation (V)", x = "Distance (D)") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "black") +
  
  # Other visual changes
  scale_colour_manual(name = "Group", values = pal) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(V), cols = vars(D), as.table = FALSE,
             scales = "free", switch = "both") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1, 
        text = element_text(size = 15),
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom")

```



## Theoretical power curves
```{r}
#| out-width: 100%
# load simulated models
load("data/glmer_models.rda")
load("data/theoretical_models.rda")
# load("data/average_fit.rda")

name_distance <- function(string) {
  paste0("Distance: \n", string)
}

LINES <- c("T-test" = "longdash", "Moran's I" = "dotdash")


theoretical_models |>
  filter(!D==0) |>
  mutate(line_id = interaction(test, plot_type, correct_number)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=V, y=power_random, group = line_id, linetype = test)) +
  geom_line(linewidth=0.3, colour = "black") +
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(legend.position="top", 
        legend.direction ="horizontal",
        text=element_text(size=10), 
        strip.text.x=element_text(size=8),
        strip.text.y=element_text(size=8),
        legend.text = element_text(size=8)) +
  guides(colour = "none") + 
  facet_wrap(~D, nrow = 1,
             labeller = labeller(D = name_distance)) +
  labs(x = "Standard Deviation", y = "Power",
       linetype = "Classical Test") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = LINES) 

```

## Aside on `ggdibbler`
A generalised uncertainty visualisation framework

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 15
#| out-width: 90%
#| fig-pos: "t"
#| dev: "png"

set.seed(10)
# any data edits
# GRAPH DF
uncertain_edges <- tibble::tibble(from = sample(5, 20, TRUE),
                                  to = sample(5, 20, TRUE),
                                  weight = runif(20)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(from, to) |>
  dplyr::mutate(to = distributional::dist_sample(list(sample(seq(from=max(1,to-1), 
                                                                 to = min(to+1, 5)), 
                                                             replace = TRUE)))) |>
  ungroup()
graph_sample <- uncertain_edges |>
  sample_expand(times=50) |>
  as_tbl_graph()
jitter = position_jitter(width=0.03, height=0.03)

# geom_sf data
Aust_map <- ozmap_data(data = "states", quiet = TRUE) |>
  group_by(NAME) |>
  mutate(value = dist_normal(mu = rnorm(1, 30, 10), rexp(1, 0.3))) |>
  ungroup()


ppie <- ggplot(uncertain_mpg, aes(x="")) +
  geom_bar_sample(aes(fill = class), times = 50, alpha=1.2/50,
                  position = "stack_identity",
                  width = 1)+
  theme_void() +
  scale_fill_gdocs() +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  theme(legend.position="none",
        aspect.ratio=1) +
  ggtitle("b. pie chart")

psf <- ggplot(data = Aust_map, aes(geometry = geometry, fill = value)) + 
  geom_sf_sample(times = 300, linewidth = 0) +
  #theme_void() +
  theme_map() +
  theme(legend.position="none") +
  geom_sf(fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5, colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_acton() + 
  scale_x_continuous_distribution(limits = c(111,155)) +
  ggtitle("d. choropleth map")

pgraph <- ggraph(graph_sample, weights = weight) + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(group=drawID), position=jitter, alpha=0.01, 
                 colour = "#cc3311") + 
  theme_void() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1) +
  geom_node_point(size=3) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1, legend.position="none") +
  ggtitle("f. network diagram")

pcount <- ggplot(uncertain_mpg, aes(cty, hwy)) +
  geom_count_sample(alpha=0.05, times=30, colour = "#FD9A44") +
  theme_few() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1, legend.position="none") +
  ggtitle("e. bubble chart")

phist <- ggplot(smaller_uncertain_diamonds, aes(carat, fill = cut)) +
  geom_histogram_sample(position="stack_dodge", alpha=1, times=30) +
  theme_few() +
  scale_fill_discreterainbow() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1, legend.position="none") +
  ggtitle("c. histogram")

pline <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) + 
  geom_abline_sample(intercept = dist_normal(37, 1.8), colour = "#9970AB",
                     slope = dist_normal(-5, 0.56), 
                     times=30, alpha=0.5) +
  geom_point(colour = "black") + 
  theme_few() +
  theme(aspect.ratio=1, legend.position = "none") +
  ggtitle("a. line plot")

pline +  ppie + phist + psf  + pcount + pgraph 
```

## Mathematical findings of `ggdibbler`
According to the formalisation, the information in the pixel and transparency map should be the same

```{r}

p1 <- ggplot(uncertain_mpg, aes(class)) + 
  geom_bar_sample(aes(fill = drv),
                  position = "stack_dodge")+
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position="none", aspect.ratio=1)+
  scale_fill_discrete_sequential(palette = "viridis") +
  ggtitle("Pixelation")

p2 <- ggplot(uncertain_mpg, aes(class)) + 
  geom_bar_sample(aes(fill = drv), alpha=0.15,
                  position = "stack_identity")+
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position="none", aspect.ratio=1)+
  scale_fill_discrete_sequential(palette = "viridis") +
  ggtitle("Transparency")



p1 | p2

```

:::::

## Hypothesis
:::: {.incremental}

This stimuli design leads to three hypothesis

1. The Choropleth and Bivariate maps will have no signal modulation
2. The VSUP map will have signal modulation, but not in a way that is statistically sensible 
2. The pixel and transparency maps will perform sensible signal modulation and be the same

::::

# Results


## Choropleth - data

![](images/choro_5x5.png){fig-align="center"}



## Choropleth - power curves

```{r}
#| out-width: 100%

map_type = "Choropleth"
pcol = gpal[1]

glmer_models |>
  filter(!D==0,
         plot_type %in% map_type) |>
  mutate(line_id = interaction(plot_type, id)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=V,  group = line_id)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = power_random), colour = pcol,
            linewidth=0.3, alpha=0.3) +
  geom_line(data = theoretical_models |>
              filter(!D==0, plot_type %in% map_type) |>
              mutate(line_id = interaction(test, plot_type, correct_number)),
            aes(y=power_random, linetype = test),
            linewidth=0.3, colour = "black") +
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(legend.position="top", 
        legend.direction ="horizontal",
        text=element_text(size=10), 
        strip.text.x=element_text(size=8),
        strip.text.y=element_text(size=8),
        legend.text = element_text(size=8)) +
  guides(colour = "none") + 
  facet_wrap(~D, nrow = 1,
             labeller = labeller(D = name_distance)) +
  labs(x = "Standard Deviation", y = "Power",
       linetype = "Classical Test") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = LINES) 

```

##  Returning to our hypothesis
:::: {.incremental}

1. The Choropleth and Bivariate maps will have no signal modulation: **Confirmed**
2. The VSUP map will have signal modulation, but not in a way that is statistically sensible: **Confirmed**  
2. The pixel and transparency maps will be the same in how well they perform signal modulation and should align with standard hypothesis tests: **Confirmed**

::::



# Conclusion

## What did we learn?
:::: {.incremental}

- It is important to know if you are evaluating uncertainty as signal or noise
- Power curve analysis is required to assess uncertainty as signal
- Visualising distributions as samples is the only approach that leads to sensible signal modulation

::::

## Back to walktober!

```{r}
# Plot0B
options(scipen = 999)
ggplot(my_suburbs) +
  geom_sf_sample(data = suburb_walk, linewidth=0, times=100,
                 aes(geometry= geometry, fill = steps_dist)) +
  geom_sf(aes(geometry= geometry), fill=NA) +
  theme_map()  +
  ggtitle("Average steps per day by Melbourne Suburb") + 
  labs(fill = "Average steps per day") +
  scale_fill_continuous_sequential(palette = "Magenta", rev = TRUE)

```
